L1@P0: Lecture #2
L2@P0: Fall 2025

L4@P0: 2 Elliptic curves as abelian groups
L5@P0: In Lecture 1 we defined an elliptic curve as a smooth projective curve of genus 1 with a
L6@P0: distinguished rational point. An equivalent definition is that an elliptic curve is an abelian
L7@P0: variety of dimension one. An abelian variety is a smooth projective variety equipped with a
L8@P0: group structure defined by rational maps (we will make this definition more precise below).
L9@P0: Remarkably, the fact that we are working with projective varieties rather than affine varieties
L10@P0: forces the group operation to be commutative, which is why they are called abelian varieties.
L11@P0: In this lecture we will prove that elliptic curves are abelian varieties by explicitly deriving
L12@P0: the rational maps that define the group law. In the course of doing so we will verify that
L13@P0: they do in fact satisfy the axioms required of a group operation.
L14@P0: 2.1 The group law for Weierstrass curves
L15@P0: Recall from Lecture 1 that the group law for an elliptic curve defined by a Weierstrass
L16@P0: equation is given by the following rule:
L17@P0: Three points on a line sum to zero, which is the point at infinity.
L18@P0: For convenience let us assume we are working over a field k whose characteristic is not 2
L19@P0: or 3. In this case we may assume that we are working with an elliptic curve E/k defined by
L20@P0: a short Weierstrass equation
L21@P0: E : y
L22@P0: 2 = x3 + Ax + B.
L23@P0: The case of a general Weierstrass equation y
L24@P0: 2+a1xy+a3y = x3+a2x2+a4x+a6 is essentially
L25@P0: the same, but the formulas are slightly more complicated; see [8, III.2.3] for details and a
L26@P0: proof that every elliptic curve can be defined by a Weierstrass equation.
L27@P0: Recall that although we typically specify our curves using an affine equation in the
L28@P0: variables x and y, we are really working with the corresponding projective curve, which in
L29@P0: this case is given by the homogeneous equation
L30@P0: E : y
L31@P0: 2
L32@P0: z = x
L33@P0: 3 + Axz2 + Bz3
L34@P0: .
L35@P0: In order to specify an elliptic curve we need not only an equation defining the curve, but
L36@P0: also a distinguished rational point, which acts as the identity of the group. For curves in
L37@P0: Weierstrass form we always take the point O := (0 : 1 : 0) at infinity as our distinguished
L38@P0: point; this is the unique point on the curve E that lies on the line z = 0 at infinity: if z = 0
L39@P0: then x = 0 and we may assume y = 1 after scaling the projective point (0 : y : 0) by 1/y;
L40@P0: note that x = z = 0 forces y ̸= 0, since (0 : 0 : 0) is (by definition) not a projective point.
L41@P0: Every point P ̸= O on the curve E thus has a nonzero z-coordinate which we can scale
L42@P0: to be 1, and we use the notation P = (x0, y0) := (x0 : y0 : 1) to denote these affine points.
L43@P0: Notice that the point Q = (x0, −y0) also lies on the curve E, and the projective line through
L44@P0: P and Q is defined by x = x0z, which also passes through O = (0 : 1 : 0). The three points
L45@P0: P, Q, O lie on a line, so P + Q + O = P + Q = O, and therefore Q = −P.
L46@P0: Commutativity of the group law follows immediately from our definition, but associativity is not obvious. We will give two proofs. The first is geometric and depends on a genericity
L47@P0: assumption that does not apply in special cases, but the proof is short and it provides some
L48@P0: intuition as to why the group law is associative. The second is algebraic and handles all
L49@P0: cases over any field whose characteristic is not 2 or 3, but we will rely on the computer
L50@P0: algebra system Sage to do the heavy lifting. A formally verified proof of associativity that
L51@P0: works in all characteristics is now available in the Lean mathlib library [1, 6].
L52@P0-1: Lecture by Andrew Sutherland2.1.1 A geometric proof of associativity in the generic case
L53@P1: This is an adaptation of the proof in [4, p. 28]. Let P, Q, R be points on an elliptic curve

L55@P1: over ¯k then it is certainly also associative when we restrict to k). We shall also assume that
L56@P1: P, Q, R, and the zero point O are all in general position. This means that in the diagram
L57@P1: below there are no relationships among the points other than those that necessarily exist by
L58@P1: construction; in particular the eight points P, Q, R, O, ±(P + Q), ±(Q + R) are distinct and
L59@P1: no three are collinear.

L105@P2: the coordinates of P and Q. If either P or Q is the point O at infinity, then R is simply
L106@P2: the other point, so we assume that P and Q are affine points P = (x1, y1) and Q = (x2, y2).
L107@P2: There are two cases.

L109@P2: equation y − y1 = m(x − x1) for P Q. This line is not vertical, so it intersects the curve
